title: Problem Design - Disguised Problems
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane presents the disguised problem as one of his favourite formative assessment tools. Disguised problems arise because curricula pose questions the same way every time and because it is valuable to probe beyond Depth of Knowledge 1. The idea is to ask for a familiar concept in a slightly different form, so students cannot run a memorised procedure and must think about the concept. He offers examples from the Pythagorean Theorem, scientific notation, expression evaluation, trapezoid area and volume, noting how many students stumbled. He closes by saying one or two such problems at key points are a modest but useful tool for finding where understanding stands.
points: Disguised problems vary the surface form of a familiar question to disrupt mindless procedure and test whether students understand the underlying concept.
They arise from curricula that always ask questions the same way and from the need to go beyond Depth of Knowledge 1 recall.
The method students choose, such as slogging through arithmetic instead of simplifying, is itself diagnostic data about their knowledge.
Used sparingly at key points in practice, they make students pause and think about what a concept means, supporting flexible later use.
quotes: One of my favorite formative assessment tools is a disguised problem. These problems come from two places. First is the tendency of math curriculum to ask certain questions the same way every time, such that students are confused when they see a very slight variation on the same question. Second is the value in probing beyond Depth of Knowledge 1, such that students cannot repeat the same procedure to obtain an answer and are pushed to think about the underlying concept.

Disguised problems try to disrupt mindless procedure and force students to think flexibly about concepts. They are not meant to be complex, challenging questions--just to ask a student to apply a concept in a different way to make sure they understand it.

Too many Pythagorean Theorem questions are asked the same way. I was shocked by how many students struggled to find the diagonal from A to E on this rectangle -- after showing fluency with straightforward right triangle questions.

Operations with scientific notation are easy to have students over-practice and disconnect from what the numbers actually mean. While any student learning scientific notation is likely to be able to answer this question without using scientific notation, the method they use is an illuminating piece of data on where their knowledge is.
Volume is easy to oversimplify into a set of formulas. Throw a slight variation that asks for the volume in a different way, and see if they can still find it.

Disguised problems are not the be-all-end-all of formative assessment, but asking students one or two at key points as they practice a concept or skill is an incredibly value tool in learning where their understanding is. Most importantly, in my view, it forces a student to pause and think for a moment about what a concept actually means, and allows them to apply their knowledge more flexibly in the future.
